splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability under ERISA must be locked in by the end of the prior plan year or may be selected afterward. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and courts lack authority to extend the term beyond what Congress prescribed.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under § 2244(b)(1) from raising any claim they previously presented in a successive § 2255 motion, in addition to the separate requirements in § 2255(h). If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress may have intended.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring any claim previously presented.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions; they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s own requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The outcome determines whether election-rule challenges can be litigated before an election or must wait until afterward, with significant implications for voting administration nationwide.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge state election rules pre-election based on competitive injury or vote-dilution theories.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate for federal office lacks Article III standing to challenge state election laws allowing extended ballot-receipt deadlines because the alleged injury is too speculative or generalized.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions that affect criminal liability or sentencing.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the rule of lenity takes priority over deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations of ambiguous criminal or sentencing provisions. The Third Circuit held that deference trumps lenity, while at least the Fourth, Fifth, and Eleventh Circuits hold that lenity trumps deference. Post-Loper Bright, this question has taken on renewed significance.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that courts should defer to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations of ambiguous criminal or sentencing provisions even when the rule of lenity would favor the defendant.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes priority over deference to agency or Commission interpretations when construing ambiguous criminal or sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through delegated interpretation.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any single criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision means 'and' or 'or.' This determines whether defendants must meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether possessing any one criterion is disqualifying. The split leads to disparate sentencing outcomes for identically situated defendants depending on geographic location.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' as conjunctive.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any single criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary (Application Note 1) to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2 can expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which includes conspiracy and other inchoate offenses in the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a permissible authoritative interpretation of the guideline or an impermissible expansion beyond the text. This split affects career-offender designations and sentencing ranges for many federal defendants.

positions.label: Commentary is authoritative — inchoate offenses included
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1's inclusion of inchoate offenses like conspiracy in the definition of 'controlled substance offense' is an authoritative interpretation of the guideline entitled to deference under Stinson, even after Kisor.

positions.label: Commentary cannot expand guideline text — inchoate offenses excluded
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses like conspiracy, and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline beyond its text, especially after Kisor's narrowing of deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule covers substances not listed on the federal schedule.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in § 4B1.2(b) requires the substance to be federally scheduled or whether any state-law drug offense qualifies. The Eighth Circuit holds there is no federal-law limitation, while other circuits require the substance to be federally controlled, creating disparate sentencing outcomes.

positions.label: No federal-schedule limitation
positions.summary: Holds that 'controlled substance offense' under § 4B1.2(b) includes any offense under state law, even if the particular substance is not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

positions.label: Federal-schedule limitation applies
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance at issue is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's changes to mandatory minimums, can constitute or contribute to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for a sentence reduction under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in law can serve as a basis for compassionate release. The Eighth Circuit categorically bars such changes from contributing to an extraordinary-and-compelling finding, while other circuits permit courts to consider them, particularly after the Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive sentencing changes as part of the extraordinary-and-compelling analysis, particularly in combination with other factors, and that the Sentencing Commission's policy statement in § 1B1.13(b)(6) authorizes such consideration.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions of confinement or BOP decisions regarding the terms of their imprisonment must proceed via habeas corpus or may bring civil rights claims, and relatedly whether habeas is the exclusive remedy for challenges affecting the duration of confinement.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy for prisoners challenging BOP decisions that affect the fact, duration, or conditions of confinement, or whether civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens or the APA) are also available. This affects federal prisoners' ability to challenge BOP decisions on First Step Act time credits and prerelease custody.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for duration-of-confinement challenges
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner challenges the fact or duration of confinement, habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy, precluding civil rights or APA claims.

positions.label: Both habeas and civil rights claims are available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring civil rights or APA claims to challenge conditions or terms of confinement even when habeas might also be available, particularly where the challenge does not seek immediate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release at revocation proceedings, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of trust and not as punishment for the underlying violation conduct.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether supervised release revocation sentences may serve a punitive purpose for the violation conduct itself. The Sixth Circuit's precedent in United States v. Lewis allows district courts expressly to punish defendants for violations, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split with courts that view revocation as addressing only the breach of the court's trust.

positions.label: Revocation may serve punitive purpose
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider punishing the defendant for the violation conduct itself when imposing a revocation sentence for supervised release violations.

positions.label: Revocation addresses breach of trust, not punishment
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should be premised on the defendant's breach of trust with the court, not as punishment for the new violation conduct, consistent with the purpose of supervised release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal deadline for filing a notice of appeal applies to an order resolving a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees, although filed in a criminal case, is a civil matter subject to the 30-day civil appeal deadline or a criminal matter subject to the 14-day criminal appeal deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies because the motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, and therefore the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion arises in a criminal case and is therefore subject to the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtors upon a good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether property appreciation between filing and conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtors. The Ninth Circuit holds that appreciation belongs to the estate, while other courts interpret § 348(f)(1)(A) as protecting debtors' post-petition equity gains.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the broad scope of § 541(a) means post-petition appreciation in property value inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtors
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) protects good-faith converting debtors by treating post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation as belonging to the debtors rather than the estate, consistent with the statute's structure and legislative history.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine as 'effectively unreviewable' after final judgment.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether denials of motions to seal medical records satisfy the collateral order doctrine for immediate appellate review. The D.C. Circuit held that medical privacy constitutes a value of 'high order' warranting immediate review, while other circuits have declined to extend the collateral order doctrine to sealing disputes.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that an order denying a motion to seal documents referencing medical treatments and diagnoses is immediately appealable because medical privacy is a value of high order that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine because post-judgment remedies remain available and such orders do not implicate rights sufficiently important to justify interlocutory appeal.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to review the Second Circuit's approach to legal questions about discrimination liability and remedies in business establishments, indicating a circuit split or unsettled question warranting review. The decision may impact hospitality, retail, and service industries nationwide.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied legal standards for discrimination or unfair treatment claims in hospitality contexts that the Supreme Court found sufficiently problematic or divergent to warrant review.

positions.label: Contrary approach
positions.summary: Other circuits apply different standards for evaluating discrimination claims in business establishments, creating the split that led to certiorari.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
